facts.title: Named After Goblins
facts.text: The name cobalt comes from the German word "Kobold," meaning goblin or evil spirit. Medieval Saxon miners blamed these mischievous sprites when a bluish ore poisoned them and yielded no useful metal despite looking like valuable silver or copper ore. The toxic fumes were actually arsenic released when the cobalt-arsenic minerals were smelted.

facts.title: A Swedish First
facts.text: In 1735 the Swedish chemist Georg Brandt isolated cobalt, proving the blue color in glass and ceramics came from a new metal, not from bismuth as many believed. This made cobalt the first new metal discovered since antiquity, when only seven metals like gold, silver, and iron were known. Brandt's work helped open the door to modern systematic chemistry.

facts.title: Blue That Lasts Millennia
facts.text: Cobalt compounds have colored glass and pottery a vivid blue for over 4,000 years, appearing in ancient Egyptian and Chinese artifacts long before anyone knew cobalt was an element. The pigment cobalt blue (cobalt aluminate) was perfected in 1802 and prized by painters like Maxfield Parrish and Vincent van Gogh. Just a tiny amount of cobalt oxide tints a large batch of glass deep blue.

facts.title: One Of Three Magnetic Metals
facts.text: Cobalt is one of only three elements that are ferromagnetic at room temperature, alongside iron and nickel. It has the highest Curie temperature of any metal at about 1,121 degrees Celsius, meaning it keeps its magnetism at extreme heat better than iron or nickel. This makes cobalt essential in powerful permanent magnets such as alnico and samarium-cobalt alloys used in motors and sensors.

facts.title: The Vitamin B12 Core
facts.text: Cobalt sits at the very center of vitamin B12 (cobalamin), making it the only metal known to be required inside a vitamin. This nutrient is essential for forming red blood cells, building DNA, and keeping the nervous system healthy, and a deficiency causes pernicious anemia. Humans cannot make B12 themselves, so we rely on bacteria that build it atom by atom around a single cobalt ion.

facts.title: A Cancer-Fighting Isotope
facts.text: The artificial isotope cobalt-60 emits high-energy gamma rays and has a half-life of about 5.27 years. Since the 1950s, cobalt-60 "bombs" have delivered radiation therapy to shrink tumors, and the same rays sterilize medical equipment and preserve food. It is produced by bombarding ordinary cobalt-59 with neutrons inside a nuclear reactor.

facts.title: Powering Your Phone
facts.text: Cobalt is a key ingredient in the lithium-ion batteries that run smartphones, laptops, and electric cars, where it stabilizes the cathode and boosts energy density. More than 70 percent of the world's mined cobalt comes from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, often as a byproduct of copper and nickel mining. The surging demand for electric vehicles has made cobalt one of the most strategically important metals of the 21st century.

facts.title: Built To Take The Heat
facts.text: Superalloys based on cobalt keep their strength at temperatures that would weaken most metals, so they line the hottest parts of jet engines and gas turbines. Cobalt-chromium alloys are also hard, corrosion-resistant, and biocompatible, which is why they are used for artificial hip and knee joints and dental implants. The trade name Stellite describes wear-resistant cobalt alloys used for cutting tools and engine valves.

facts.title: Forged In Dying Stars
facts.text: Cobalt is created deep inside massive stars and is flung across space when those stars explode as supernovae. Much of the cobalt in the universe actually begins as radioactive nickel-56, which decays into cobalt-56 and then into stable iron-56, powering the fading light of a supernova for months. Earth's cobalt is concentrated in the planet's core and scattered through its crust at only about 25 parts per million.

facts.title: The Color-Changing Trick
facts.text: Cobalt chloride is famous for changing color with humidity, turning pink when wet and blue when dry, which is why it once coated "weather" novelty cards and silica-gel drying packets. This reversible shift happens because water molecules attach to and detach from the cobalt ion, rearranging how it absorbs light. Chemistry teachers still use the effect as a vivid, hands-on way to demonstrate hydration and equilibrium.
